title: Operation Mistral 2: The Recapture of Jajce
sources: ICTY Gotovina et al. Trial Judgment (IT-06-90-T)
content:
When Jajce fell to VRS forces in late October 1992, it represented one of the most bitter early defeats of the war. The historic town — site of the 1943 AVNOJ conference that had shaped Yugoslavia's postwar constitution — was lost amid mutual recriminations between HVO and ARBiH commanders who had failed to coordinate its defense. Tens of thousands of civilians fled. For nearly three years afterward, Jajce sat behind VRS lines, a symbol of the fractured Bosniak-Croat alliance and the military dominance the Bosnian Serb army had established across western Bosnia. On 13 September 1995, it was retaken.

Operation Mistral 2 was the direct successor to Operation Storm and the broader Croatian military campaign that had reshaped the strategic landscape of the western Balkans in August 1995. The same elite formations that had driven through the Krajina — the HV 4th and 7th Guards Brigades — now pushed northward from the Grahovo-Glamoč corridor into the heart of VRS-held territory. The operation was coordinated with HVO forces and received tacit support from the ARBiH, reflecting the operational framework of the Federation alliance.

The VRS defensive position in western Bosnia had become untenable. NATO's Operation Deliberate Force, launched on 30 August, was systematically degrading Bosnian Serb military infrastructure — communications, ammunition depots, air defenses, and command facilities. The destruction of the Krajina Serb entity in Operation Storm had eliminated the VRS's western strategic depth. The 2nd Krajina Corps, responsible for defending this vast sector, was depleted, demoralized, and unable to hold its extended lines against concentrated Croatian assault forces that enjoyed superior numbers, equipment, and momentum.

The advance was rapid. Šipovo fell first. Then Mrkonjić Grad. Croatian forces swept through a disintegrating VRS defense, capturing approximately 2,000 square kilometers in eight days. When Jajce was liberated on 13 September, the symbolic weight of the moment was enormous. A town lost in the war's darkest early months had been recaptured, vindicating the Federation alliance and demonstrating the complete reversal of the military balance that had prevailed for most of the conflict.

The ICTY proceedings in Gotovina et al. (IT-06-90-T) examined the Croatian military operations of 1995 as an interconnected campaign, from Summer '95 through Storm and into the Bosnian operations that followed. The trial addressed questions about the conduct of Croatian forces, including the treatment of Serb civilians and property in areas that came under Croatian and HVO control during these rapid advances.

The fall of western Bosnia had profound consequences for the war's endgame. Republika Srpska, which had controlled approximately 70 percent of Bosnian territory at its peak, was being compressed toward the 49 percent that the Contact Group plan had proposed as the basis for a settlement. The VRS, simultaneously battered from the air by NATO and driven back on the ground by Federation forces, could no longer sustain the territorial holdings it had seized in 1992. The recapture of Jajce was not merely a local victory — it was proof that the strategic conditions for a negotiated settlement had finally been created through military force rather than diplomatic persuasion alone.
